name: CPAP (sleep apnea)

lead: CPAP delivers air at constant pressure through a mask to keep your airway open during sleep. It is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. In appearance communities, it is discussed for the fresher, less puffy look that comes with restored sleep.

Pressurised air splints the upper airway open, which eliminates obstructive apneas in most people who use it as directed, so sleep is no longer repeatedly broken. Better sleep is what users connect to less facial puffiness. In people with sleep apnea it lowers overall cardiovascular death risk; appearance outcomes have not been tested in the sources reviewed.

paras: CPAP is a prescription device used nightly with a nasal, full-face or hybrid mask after a sleep study diagnoses apnea. Users adjust mask type and fit with their provider. Sleep quality often changes within days to weeks of consistent use.

Adherence is a major issue: about 8% stop after the first night and more than half within a year. Reported side effects include discomfort, congestion, bloating, claustrophobia and mask leaks. It is a prescription medical device and needs a diagnosis.

angle.text: CPAP keeps the airway open at night so sleep is no longer repeatedly broken, and online discussion links that restored sleep with less facial puffiness and a fresher look. It is the standard treatment for moderate to severe sleep apnea; appearance outcomes were not studied in the sources reviewed.

lead: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers pressurised air through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep. [1] It was developed in adults by Colin Sullivan, who built a machine in 1980 at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney, and Respironics began selling a commercial adult device in 1985. [1]

It is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea and, in people with sleep apnea, lowers overall risk of cardiovascular death. [1] Case series have reported reduced seizure frequency in people with epilepsy and sleep apnea who used CPAP. [2]
Looksmaxxing communities discuss CPAP for facial puffiness and appearance; no appearance studies were found.

paras: CPAP eliminates obstructive apneas in most people who use it as recommended. [1] Adherence is a major problem: about 8% quit after the first night and more than half within the first year. [1] A small series of refractory epilepsy patients with sleep apnea found that success depended largely on compliance. [2]
Users may report discomfort, nasal congestion, bloating, claustrophobia, mask leaks and mouth leaks. [1] Full-face masks and chin straps are used to manage mouth leaks. [1]

A 1994 case series of seven patients with refractory partial epilepsy and sleep apnea reported reduced seizure frequency in six after treating apnea, including four of five with CPAP. [2] No studies found examining CPAP for facial puffiness or appearance.
